hero.title: Which Diamond Shapes Are the Most Expensive—and Why?
hero.subheading: Compare colourless natural diamond shapes by typical price position, understand why round brilliants carry a premium, and learn how to evaluate value beyond shape alone.

paragraphs: The round brilliant is usually the most expensive diamond shape per carat when comparing colourless natural diamonds with similar carat weight, colour, clarity, grading reports and overall quality.

Its higher price is driven by a combination of strong market demand, the amount of rough diamond removed during cutting, strict proportion requirements and its ability to produce exceptional brilliance.

However, this does not mean every round diamond costs more than every oval, cushion or emerald-cut diamond. A large, rare or exceptionally well-cut fancy-shaped diamond can cost considerably more than a lower-quality round diamond.
The correct comparison must always be made between diamonds with similar specifications.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer
quickAnswer.question: Which diamond shape is the most expensive?
introParagraphs: The round brilliant is generally the most expensive common diamond shape per carat. More of the original rough crystal may be removed to produce a well-proportioned round diamond, while demand for the shape remains consistently strong.

Fancy shapes—including oval, pear, cushion, princess, emerald, radiant and marquise—often cost less per carat than comparable round diamonds. Their exact prices depend on demand, rarity, proportions, visual performance and how efficiently each shape can be produced from the rough diamond.

keyTakeaways.title: Key Takeaways
items: Round brilliant diamonds normally command the highest price per carat.
A diamond’s shape should never be compared without controlling for carat, colour, clarity and certification.
Fancy shapes do not follow one permanent price ranking.
Oval, pear and marquise diamonds can provide a larger face-up appearance for their weight.
Princess and radiant cuts can retain more of the original rough crystal than a round brilliant.
Fancy-shaped diamonds require visual inspection because a grading report does not describe every aspect of their appearance.
The least expensive stone is not automatically the best-value stone for a jeweller or customer.

shapeVsCut.title: Diamond Shape Versus Diamond Cut
introParagraphs: Diamond shape and diamond cut are related, but they are not the same.
Shape describes the diamond’s visible outline. Examples include round, oval, pear, emerald, cushion and marquise.
Cut quality describes how successfully the diamond’s proportions, facets and finish manage light. It affects brightness, fire, scintillation and the diamond’s overall appearance.

This distinction matters when people search for the “most expensive diamond cut”. They are often asking which diamond shape costs the most, but two diamonds of the same shape can still have very different values because of their cut quality.

whyRoundExpensive.title: Why Are Round Diamonds More Expensive?

subsections.title: 1. More of the Rough Diamond May Be Removed
paragraphsBefore: A polished diamond begins as an irregular natural crystal. The cutter must decide which shape will produce the strongest balance of beauty, weight and commercial value.
Producing a symmetrical, well-proportioned round brilliant can require the removal of more rough material than shapes that follow the original crystal more closely.
For example, the GIA explains that princess-cut diamonds may cost less per carat because cutters can retain more of the original diamond crystal.
When less polished weight remains from an expensive piece of rough, the cost associated with every retained carat increases.

subsections.title: 2. Round Brilliant Diamonds Have Consistently Strong Demand
paragraphsBefore: Round diamonds are widely used for engagement rings, earrings, pendants, side stones and classic jewellery designs. This broad commercial demand supports their pricing.

A jeweller can use a round brilliant across numerous collections and markets. Some fancy shapes appeal to a narrower customer group and may take longer to sell, even when the stone itself is attractive.

subsections.title: 3. Round Brilliants Are Designed for Strong Light Performance
paragraphsBefore: A round brilliant has a highly standardised facet structure designed to produce brightness, fire and scintillation.
The GIA diamond-shape guide describes the round brilliant as the only shape that currently receives an overall GIA cut grade from Excellent to Poor.

This standardised grading system gives buyers an additional way to compare round diamonds. Fancy shapes still receive information such as polish, symmetry, measurements and proportions, but their complete visual performance cannot be reduced to one overall GIA cut grade.

subsections.title: 4. High-Quality Cutting Requires Precision
paragraphsBefore: Small differences in table size, depth, pavilion angle, crown angle, girdle thickness and facet alignment can affect the appearance of a round diamond.
Cutters must balance polished weight against light performance. Retaining extra weight may increase the carat number, but poor proportions can leave a diamond looking dark, small or less lively.
Well-cut round diamonds therefore carry value not only because of their shape, but also because of the precision required to produce them.

ovalSecondMost.title: Are Oval Diamonds the Second Most Expensive Shape?
introParagraphs: Not always.
Oval diamonds are often among the more expensive fancy shapes because they are popular, elegant and can look large for their carat weight. However, oval prices vary significantly according to:
bullets: Availability within a particular carat range
closingParagraphs: A lively oval with an attractive outline and minimal bow-tie may command a stronger price than an oval with the same report grades but weaker visual performance.

The GIA’s research into oval, pear and marquise diamonds also demonstrates how outline preferences and length-to-width ratios vary. This is one reason fancy-shaped diamonds should be inspected visually instead of selected from report grades alone.

pearMarquise.title: Pear and Marquise Diamonds: Price Versus Visible Size
introParagraphs: Pear and marquise diamonds often offer strong face-up presence because their weight is distributed across an elongated outline.
A one-carat marquise may look larger from above than a one-carat round diamond, even though both stones have the same weight. Pear diamonds can provide a similar visual advantage.
However, buyers should inspect:
bullets: Very thin areas of the girdle

cushionRadiantPrincess.title: Cushion, Radiant and Princess Diamonds
introParagraphs: These shapes usually cost less per carat than comparable round brilliants, but their appearance can vary considerably.

subsections.title: Cushion-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Cushions can be square, rectangular or elongated. They can also have different facet patterns, ranging from broad, defined flashes to a denser “crushed ice” appearance.
Two cushions with identical carat, colour and clarity grades may look completely different.

subsections.title: Radiant-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Radiant diamonds combine a rectangular or square outline with a brilliant-style facet arrangement. They can provide strong sparkle while generally costing less per carat than round diamonds.
The outline, depth, light return and concentration of colour can influence the value of an individual radiant.

subsections.title: Princess-Cut Diamonds
paragraphsBefore: Princess diamonds can retain more of the original rough crystal, helping them offer competitive prices. Buyers should still inspect corner durability, girdle thickness, symmetry and areas of light leakage.

emeraldAsscher.title: Emerald and Asscher Cuts
introParagraphs: Emerald and Asscher diamonds use step-cut facets rather than the smaller brilliant-style facets found in round and radiant diamonds.
They may be priced below comparable round diamonds, but selecting a beautiful step cut can require spending more on colour or clarity.

Large, open facets can make inclusions easier to see. They can also reveal colour more clearly than a brilliant-style facet pattern. Weakly proportioned stones may show windowing, dark areas or a small face-up appearance for their weight.
This means a buyer might save money on the shape premium but choose a higher clarity or colour grade to achieve the desired appearance.

heartShaped.title: Are Heart-Shaped Diamonds Expensive?
introParagraphs: Heart-shaped diamonds have highly variable prices.

Demand is narrower than for round or oval diamonds, but cutting a balanced heart shape requires skill. The two lobes should appear even, the cleft should be clear, and the point should align with the centre of the stone.
Well-shaped hearts can be harder to find in certain specifications. A poorly shaped heart may cost less, but the lower price does not make it better value.

mostExpensiveBest.title: Does the Most Expensive Shape Mean the Best Diamond?
introParagraphs: No.
A round brilliant may be the most expensive shape per carat, but that does not make it the correct choice for every customer, jewellery design or stock plan.
For buyers who prioritise maximum brilliance and broad market familiarity, a well-cut round brilliant may justify its premium.
For buyers who want a larger visual appearance, distinctive design or lower price per carat, a well-selected fancy shape may provide better value.
The best diamond is the stone that meets the required appearance, quality, budget and commercial purpose—not simply the one with the highest price.

howToCompare.title: How to Compare Diamond Prices by Shape Correctly
introParagraphs: Before deciding that one shape is cheaper than another, compare the diamonds on an equal basis.

subsections.title: Use the Same Diamond Type
paragraphsBefore: Do not compare the price of a natural diamond with a lab-grown diamond. Their supply structures and market prices are fundamentally different.

subsections.title: Keep the Carat Range Consistent
paragraphsBefore: Compare stones within the same carat range. Diamond prices can rise noticeably around popular weight thresholds such as 0.50, 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 carats.

subsections.title: Match Colour and Clarity
paragraphsBefore: A lower-colour or lower-clarity round diamond may cost less than a high-colour, high-clarity fancy shape. That does not prove the round shape is cheaper.

subsections.title: Review the Grading Laboratory
paragraphsBefore: Compare grading reports from recognised laboratories and verify that the report matches the diamond being offered.

subsections.title: Calculate Price Per Carat
paragraphsBefore: Use the following calculation:
Price per carat = total loose-diamond price ÷ carat weight
Price per carat helps normalise comparisons, but it still does not measure beauty, proportions or saleability.

subsections.title: Compare Face-Up Measurements
paragraphsBefore: Review the length, width and depth—not only carat weight. This will show whether the diamond carries excess weight below the girdle or offers good visible spread.

finalAnswer.title: Final Answer: Which Diamond Shape Costs the Most?
introParagraphs: The round brilliant is normally the most expensive common diamond shape per carat when all other important quality factors are comparable.
Its premium comes from strong demand, lower rough retention in many cutting situations, precise manufacturing requirements and its established reputation for brilliance.
Fancy shapes can cost less per carat and may provide greater visible size, but there is no single permanent ranking for every oval, pear, cushion, emerald or radiant diamond.
Always compare the complete stone—not only its shape or discount.

items.question: What is the most expensive diamond shape?
items.answer: The round brilliant is generally the most expensive common diamond shape per carat when compared with natural diamonds of similar carat, colour, clarity and quality.

items.question: Why are round diamonds more expensive?
items.answer: Round diamonds usually carry a premium because producing them can remove more of the original rough crystal, market demand is consistently strong and precise proportions are required for high-quality light performance.

items.question: Is an oval diamond more expensive than a round diamond?
items.answer: A comparable oval normally costs less per carat than a round brilliant. However, an exceptional oval may cost more than a lower-quality round diamond because price also depends on carat, colour, clarity, proportions and availability.

items.question: What is the cheapest diamond shape?
items.answer: There is no permanently cheapest shape. Princess, cushion, emerald and some other fancy shapes can cost less per carat than comparable rounds, but the lowest-priced individual stone may have weaker colour, clarity, proportions or visual performance.

items.question: Which diamond shape looks the largest?
items.answer: Marquise, oval and pear diamonds often look larger face-up than round diamonds of the same carat weight because their elongated outlines spread weight across a greater visible area.

items.question: Does diamond shape affect price per carat?
items.answer: Yes. Shape affects rough-diamond retention, cutting complexity, market demand, availability and face-up appearance. These factors can all influence price per carat.

items.question: Does the most expensive diamond shape sparkle the most?
items.answer: A well-cut round brilliant is designed for strong brightness, fire and scintillation. However, price alone does not guarantee sparkle. Poorly proportioned round diamonds may perform worse than well-selected fancy shapes.

items.question: Why do GIA reports not show an overall cut grade for most fancy shapes?
items.answer: As of July 2026, GIA gives an overall cut grade to standard round brilliant diamonds, while fancy shapes receive measurements, polish, symmetry and other information. Their varied outlines and facet arrangements require additional visual assessment.

items.question: How should jewellers compare diamond-shape prices?
items.answer: Jewellers should compare diamonds with similar carat, colour, clarity, certification and quality, then review price per carat, face-up measurements, visual performance and total landed cost.

items.question: Do the same shape-price rules apply to fancy-colour diamonds?
items.answer: Not necessarily. In fancy-colour diamonds, colour rarity, strength and distribution can influence value more than the usual colourless-diamond shape hierarchy.

finalTakeaway.title: Compare the Complete Diamond—Not Only Its Shape
introParagraphs: Round brilliants usually command the highest price per carat among common colourless shapes, but the best commercial choice depends on appearance, demand, setting needs and total landed cost.
Use equal-basis comparisons, inspect fancy shapes visually, and select the stone that fits your customer and stock plan.
